newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria wants privatisation at its own pace.
newsitem.headline: Algeria wants privatisation at its own pace.

text.p: Algeria says it will move at a moderate pace to sell state-run businesses, turning down World Bank experts' recipe for mass privatisation to speed up transition to a free economy market.

"Privatisation in Algeria will be made case by case to avoid any haste," said Abderrahmane Mebtoul, the free market academic crusader who was appointed last month to oversee privatisation of Algeria's estimated 1,350 state-owned saleable enterprises.
Mebtoul, head of the newly created Privatisation Council, was quoted by the Algerian official news agency APS as saying on Tuesday:
"It is a matter of carrying out a privatisation which will ensure global efficiency and social equity with the aim of avoiding social upheaval jeopardising all the reform process".

Mebtoul was clearly reacting to World Bank experts who lectured Algerian managers and economic officials involved in the privatisaiton on how previous sell-offs were handled worldwide, including success stories in some former communist states.
One World Bank expert, quoted on Monday by APS, said the best scenario for Algeria was to put on sale 300 enterprises, as a first batch in a privatisation programme.

World Bank regional director for the Maghreb, Daniel Ritchie, in an interview with Algeria's Liberte newspaper late in September, urged Algeria to speed up the process by "popular privatisation through the technique of widescale selling-off by vouchers".

The two-day debates in a conference on privatisation this week attended by World Bank experts showed a large consensus among Algerians, officials and private businessmen as well as unionised workers and public sector managers, over a cautious path in the privatisation.
They clearly feared that quick privatisation, if successful, would put more people out of work, fuelling the country's turmoil amid nearly five years of civil strife in which 50,000 people have died.
The authorities announced on Monday that more state-owned companies would soon be offered for sale and that they would shut down some money-losing small businesses run by local authorities.
But they refused to reveal any numbers.
